papers.title: Dopaminergic reward signals shape foraging decisions through learned value expectations
papers.abstract: A fundamental function of the nervous system is to direct animals towards life-sustaining resources and enable adaptive strategies for acquiring them. Foraging, the challenge of securing these resources from the environment, requires making decisions that balance local gains against costs, opening a window on value-based decision making in ecological context. Yet despite the centrality of foraging in life, the algorithms and neural mechanisms underlying foraging decisions are not well understood. We studied mice making stay-or-leave patch foraging decisions for water across poor- and rich-resource environments with dynamic local reward outcomes. We found that mice integrate immediate rewards, local reward history, and reward (i.e. value) expectations to guide foraging decisions, favoring greater time investment in rich-environment patches. Computational models revealed influence of a time-varying bias which mirrored the shape of a learned value function. Consistent with a reinforcement learning mechanism, dopamine in the ventral striatum signaled a temporal-difference reward prediction error, which could be used as a teaching signal to construct value functions, and calibrated optogenetic manipulation of dopamine to create fictive reward signals recapitulated the value-related decision bias. Taken together, our results shed new light on the neurocomputational basis of foraging, revealing a novel role for value expectations in dynamic environments. Further, they establish generalized function of biological reinforcement learning in ecological context, demonstrating a specific role for the canonical dopamine reward circuit in shaping temporally resolved value expectations to guide behavior and cognition. The unification of this framework with foraging opens a new avenue to elucidate principles of how animals learn and dynamically adjust cognitive strategies for real-world ecological problems.

papers.title: Constricted pupil states index neural replay during wakeful rest in humans
papers.abstract: Neural replay has been linked to skill consolidation during wakeful rest, yet its physiological context in humans remains poorly understood. In animals, hippocampal ripples and associated replay occur more frequently within intrinsically oriented brain states associated with constricted pupils, suggesting that pupil dynamics may index neural replay events in humans. We combined magnetoencephalography-derived sequence replay with pupillometry in 25 participants learning a motor sequence across alternating intervals of practice and rest. Replay was indexed by smaller-pupil states, and replay timing clustered on the constricting phase of slow pupil fluctuations. More frequent replay accompanied larger cumulative offline gains during early learning, while smaller rest pupil was associated with better performance when practice resumed. Multivariate pupil features predicted replay-associated states across and within individuals while preceding pupil dynamics showed modest predictive ability to identify the precise onset of individual replay events. Here, we show that constricted-pupil states index neural replay during wakeful rest in humans, linking replay-associated physiology with early motor learning.

papers.title: Activation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons promotes the attribution of incentive salience to reward cues in male rats
papers.abstract: Background: Reward-associated environmental stimuli (cues) can gain incentive salience in some individuals, thereby becoming attractive, reinforcing, and instigators of motivational states. In rodents, the tendency to attribute incentive salience can be measured using a Pavlovian Conditioned Approach (PavCA) procedure, in which approach to a food cue (sign-tracking), relative to approach to the food delivery location (goal-tracking) is the operational definition of the incentive salience attributed to the cue. Growing evidence suggests that acetylcholine promotes this process, thus the current study tested the effect of activating cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain on sign- and goal-tracking during PavCA. Methods: We injected a Cre-dependent virus with excitatory Designer Receptors Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADDs) into the horizontal limb of the diagonal band of Broca of transgenic rats expressing cre-recombinase in acetylcholine containing neurons. We then injected clozapine-n-oxide (CNO) before each of eight sessions of PavCA. On the ninth session, no CNO was given to test if any effects were immediately reversible. Results: We found that activation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons increased sign-tracking over time without an overall effect on goal-tracking, relative to a control group injected with a control virus. Changes in responding from the final CNO session to the saline test did not differ between virus groups. Conclusions: This effect demonstrates that acetylcholine promotes the attribution of incentive salience to a reward-related cue. Future studies should investigate the effect of inhibiting this area on sign-tracking as well as how activation of this area influences reactivity to cues associated with other rewards such as drugs of abuse.

papers.title: A sparse neural code for acoustic targets enables speech-like vocal flexibility in parrots
papers.abstract: English speech flexibly recombines 44 phonemes into >20,000 words and limitless phrases. Here we identify a novel neural code supporting combinatorial vocal control in budgerigar parrots. Deep learning based acoustic analyses show that both English imitated and natural warble songs are composed of subsyllabic acoustic elements that are flexibly reused across acoustic contexts, analogous to phoneme reuse in words. Such reuse poses a scaling problem for songbird-inspired timing-based codes, which require distinct neural sequences for distinct syllables even when syllables share acoustic components. We identified neurons in the parrot frontal cortical nucleus MO that exhibit sparse bursts locked to reused acoustic elements independent of syllable identity, timing, or surrounding acoustic context. These results provide the first evidence for a sparse, acoustically-grounded vocal motor code that can be flexibly reused to assemble a large and combinatorial vocal repertoire.

papers.title: Inferring structural complexity from dynamical measures
papers.abstract: Complexity, commonly defined as the coexistence of integration and differentiation, is a fundamental property of thalamocortical networks and is regarded as a prerequisite for adaptive brain function and consciousness. A variety of metrics have been developed to estimate neural complexity from recorded activity and are increasingly employed in both research and clinical settings. Yet, the extent to which these measures reflect specific architectural features of the underlying circuits remains poorly understood. Here, we used Wilson-Cowan mean-field equations to simulate neural dynamics across networks spanning a broad range of architectures. By systematically rewiring connectivity, we generated graded variations in the structural integration-differentiation balance and assessed a panel of complexity measures derived either from spontaneous activity (observational metrics) or from responses to external perturbations (perturbational metrics). Observational measures exhibited markedly heterogeneous behavior: some were primarily sensitive to network integration, others to differentiation, whereas some showed limited sensitivity to architectural manipulations. In contrast, perturbational measures robustly peaked at intermediate rewiring steps and scaled with small-worldness, consistent with architectures that combine local recurrence and distributed communication. Moreover, perturbational metrics proved robust to common-driver confounds and were highest in a wake-like regime near critical instability, declining as sleep-like dynamics became more widespread across the network. Taken together, these findings map widely used empirical complexity measures onto specific network architectures, reveal dynamical factors that can bias observational estimates, and provide guidance for inferring complexity in systems whose internal organization is inaccessible, unconventional, or only partially known, including brain organoids, non-human nervous systems, and synthetic neural networks.

papers.title: An organotypic hippocampo-prefrontal co-culture model for studying long-range connectivity and circuit plasticity
papers.abstract: The hippocampal projection to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is a key component of brain networks involved in cognition and emotion. Here, we establish and validate an organotypic entorhino-hippocampo-prefrontal co-culture model that enables experimental investigation of long-range circuit connectivity and plasticity under controlled in vitro conditions. Anatomical tracing, viral labeling, and ultrastructural analyses demonstrate hippocampal axonal projections and synapse formation within the mPFC. Functional connectivity was supported by hippocampal CA1 stimulation, which evoked postsynaptic responses in 90.6% of recorded layer 2/3 mPFC pyramidal neurons. Intrinsic membrane properties and excitatory synaptic transmission were largely preserved across culture configurations. To demonstrate the experimental utility of the model, we examined the effects of selective alveus lesion and global activity blockade. Alveus lesion produced no detectable changes in the examined synaptic or intrinsic properties of mPFC neurons, whereas tetrodotoxin-mediated activity blockade increased miniature excitatory postsynaptic current frequency and reduced membrane capacitance. Together, these findings establish a versatile experimental platform for investigating long-range circuit connectivity and activity-dependent plasticity, with potential applications in mechanistic studies of neuromodulatory interventions.

papers.title: Projection populations form a dorsoventral gradient of reward representations in the lateral septum
papers.abstract: Several decades ago, the septal region was identified as the most dependable location of intracranial self-stimulation (ICSS) in the brain, but the neural substrates that mediate septal self-stimulation are still unknown. One part of the septal region, the lateral septum (LS), contributes to a number of motivated behaviors and may promote reward-seeking. However, the LS contains different anatomical subregions, complicating the characterization of its reward representations. We examine the responses of LS neurons along its dorsoventral axis using cellular resolution calcium imaging during an operant assay. We find that a greater proportion of neurons are excited in response to sucrose reward in the dorsal LS, while a greater proportion are inhibited in response to sucrose reward in the ventral LS. Additionally, we identify two distinct LS projection populations, one to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and another to the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), which are located in the dorsal and ventral regions of the LS, respectively. These two projection populations also have opposing reward responses and their corresponding optogenetic manipulation supports ICSS. These findings demonstrate how LS projection populations contribute to its functional heterogeneity, especially as it pertains to reward-seeking behavior.

papers.title: Task-general brain state dynamics relate to trial-to-trial performance and individual response strategy
papers.abstract: Behavior fluctuates from moment to moment, yet individuals also show characteristic response strategies across tasks. Whether these two levels of variation relate to common brain dynamics is unknown. Using an inside-out approach across 10 cognitive tasks during fMRI, we identified recurring brain states and related their dynamics to behavior within and between individuals. Default mode network (DMN) dominant and action mode network (AMN) dominant states occurred in all tasks. Within individuals, momentary state identity (the state occupied at a given moment) tracked trial-to-trial performance. The AMN-dominant state was associated with slower, more variable responses across tasks, whereas its relationship to accuracy depended on the task. Across individuals, switching between the two states, but not time spent in either, showed cross-task consistency, and frequent switchers showed faster, less accurate responding. Thus, distinct aspects of the same task-general brain state dynamics, momentary state identity and state switching, relate to behavior at both levels.

papers.title: Coordinated cerebellar-midbrain activity for predictive signaling during fear learning in mice
papers.abstract: Learning from experience to assess threat is crucial for survival and mental health. This function is known to involve several midbrain areas, notably the ventrolateral periaqueductal grey (vlPAG) and dorsal raphe nuclei (DRN). Recently it has been shown that fear learning involves projections from the cerebellar fastigial nucleus (FN) to the vlPAG. Here, we show using simultaneous single-unit recordings during fear conditioning that a subset of vlPAG/DRN and FN neurons acquire responses to conditioned cues following learning. Strikingly, these populations exhibit firing covariance and directional functional interactions consistent with their collaboration to the response to cues predicting threat. We also demonstrated the reciprocal monosynaptic connectivity between vlPAG/DRN and FN supporting the interactions between these structures. Together, our findings demonstrate shared dynamical activity within a network integrating midbrain and cerebellar computations during fear learning.

papers.title: Individual Differences in Sustained Attention Tune Semantic Abstraction in Neural Encoding of Narratives
papers.abstract: Neural encoding modeling for narrative comprehension -- using LLM embeddings to predict the temporal dynamics of neural activation -- is widely used to evaluate how well the brain represents certain semantic information. This approach, however, typically collapses semantic representation into a scalar fidelity score aggregated across participants, overlooking potentially rich individual differences and qualitative differences in naturalistic neural representations. In the current study, we addressed this gap by investigating how neural semantic encoding varies across individuals with sustained attention, and whether this difference is qualitative in addition to quantitative. Using fMRI data from 49 participants listening to an audiobook, Le Petit Prince, in English, we trained encoding models with GPT-2 embeddings at varying layers and forecasting lengths. Encoding models trained on high-level embeddings (from the 8th layer of GPT-2) showed significant brain-LLM alignment in 73 of 122 cortical and subcortical ROIs, concentrated in the temporal cortex and the default mode network. Functional connectivity strength in a validated connectome-based predictive model of sustained attention correlated with encoding performance in 18 ROIs, most strongly in the insula and in control and attention networks, with no ROI showing significant opposite relationship. Decomposing semantic information by levels of abstraction showed that the neural signature of sustained attention was selectively associated with a greater proportion of high-level gist information encoded in the frontoparietal and attention networks, while the opposite relationship emerged for proportion of low-level information. Sustained attention scores further predicted stronger predictive coding of upcoming narrative content across multiple networks across the whole brain (control, default mode, salience/ventral attention, limbic, and somatomotor networks). These findings suggest that sustained attention does not uniformly amplify neural semantic encoding, but instead shifts neural representations toward more compressed, gist-level formats that support anticipation of upcoming content. Individual differences in brain-LLM alignment can be a signature of representational strategy rather than noise, with potential utility for cognitive phenotyping.

papers.title: Hypothalamic plasticity for alloparenting in male mice
papers.abstract: Repeated exposure to young can induce caregiving in virgin female mice, a phenomenon known as pup sensitization, but whether virgin males can similarly acquire parental behavior and the neural mechanisms underlying this transition remain unclear. We show that 7 days of continuous pup exposure reliably converts virgin adult male mice to a parental state. This transition requires calcitonin receptor (CalcR)-expressing neurons in the medial preoptic area (MPOA): silencing MPOACalcR neurons disrupts both the acquisition and expression of paternal behavior, whereas optogenetic activation of GABAergic MPOACalcR neurons promotes caregiving in virgin males. Longitudinal two-photon calcium imaging reveals that MPOACalcR neurons develop enhanced pup-selective responses as males transition to a parental state. Moreover, CalcR signaling in the MPOA promotes synaptic potentiation and facilitates the emergence of parental behavior. These results identify an experience-dependent hypothalamic plasticity mechanism that enables parental behavior in non-father males.

papers.title: Parrots imitate song and dance with mixed vocal-gestural neural signals
papers.abstract: Humans shrug when saying "I don't know" and nod when saying "yes," yet it remains unclear how the brain coordinates vocal and gestural motor systems for learned, multimodal communication. Here we find that budgerigar parrots precisely imitate the fine temporal alignment between song and affiliative headbob gestures. Distinct colonies developed unique vocal-gestural motifs, which reorganized into new shared forms following social re-pairing. Neural recordings from the central nucleus of the anterior arcopallium (AAC), the cortical output of the parrot song system, revealed intermixed representations of vocalizations and head kinematics, including mixed selectivity at the level of single neurons. These findings show that socially learned multimodal communication is implemented by the joint representation of vocal and gestural motor signals within single neurons, revealing neural mechanisms that may extend to frontal cortical regions controlling speech and gesture in humans.

papers.title: Development of Neonatal Functional Brain Network Organisation and Its Association with Childhood Neurodevelopmental Outcomes
papers.abstract: The human brain undergoes rapid dynamic changes in the neonatal period that are essential for later cognitive and behavioural performance. Using resting-state fMRI data from 394 neonates (325 term-born, 69 preterm-born) within the first month after birth, we characterised the early development of functional network organisation, the effects of preterm birth, and the association between neonatal functional organisation and later neurodevelopmental outcomes in infancy (18 months) and childhood (4-6 years). We found increased functional integration and segregation across a wide range of functional sub-networks and increased mean functional connectivity strength (mean FCS) within the subcortical and cerebellar regions with increasing PMA at scan. Compared with term-born neonates, preterm-born neonates showed significantly lower mean FCS, functional integration and segregation globally. We further showed that whilst neonatal functional brain network organisation was not associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes measured during infancy (18 months), it was associated with later neurodevelopmental outcomes in early childhood (4-6 years). Specifically, higher functional integration and segregation at birth were linked with lower SDQ total difficulties score at 4-6 years. Our findings suggest that neonatal functional brain organisation reflects not only transient developmental processes, but also stable individual differences that provide insight into neurodevelopmental outcomes in later childhood.

papers.title: A new neural code for position: generalizable spatial maps in mouse medial frontal cortex
papers.abstract: Navigation requires the brain to encode spatial relationships that support extrapolation from explored to unexplored regions of space. We identified a novel neural code for space in the mouse medial frontal cortex (mFC) that is well suited for this form of spatial generalization. Using calcium imaging of excitatory neurons in mFC, hippocampus (dorsal CA1), and lateroventral orbitofrontal cortex (lvOFC) as mice explored a square arena with landmarks, we found that mFC activity supports extrapolation. Linear regression of the animal's x or y coordinates trained in one region of the arena generalized to a completely different region. This property was observed in mFC but not in dCA1 or lvOFC. A model in which neurons encode the squared distance from the animal to multiple landmarks explains several properties of the geometry of the mFC representation, including extrapolation. The neural map that we observed in the frontal cortex may provide a basis for vector computation in navigation and complex route planning.

papers.title: iFLiP: accessible and low-cost lifetime fiber photometry for robust longitudinal and quantitative measurements of neural dynamics
papers.abstract: Fluorescence lifetime measurements overcome the limitation of widely used intensity-based measurements in quantifying tonic activities and longitudinal changes in neural dynamics. However, while lifetime sensors are rapidly emerging, their applications have been limited by the complexity and expense of required hardware and software. Here, we report a simple, low-cost lifetime fiber photometry system, named iFLiP, that uses entirely off-the-shelf products and can be assembled without specialized expertise. We also develop software that enables turn-key operation. The integrated system can accurately monitor lifetime changes at up to 5000 Hz for days. We demonstrate the utility of iFLiP in monitoring the activity of protein kinase A (PKA) in vitro and in vivo, and uncover striatal subregion- and cell-type-specific PKA dynamics elicited by locomotion in mice. Additionally, multi-day continuous measurements in the basal forebrain reveal previously unappreciated PKA activity associated with sleep/wakefulness. Overall, iFLiP may make lifetime measurements broadly accessible in neuroscience research.

papers.title: A note on the responsiveness of neurons
papers.abstract: The time constant of biological neurons is typically around 5-20ms. This raises the question of how a system made of slow devices can generate and respond to faster signals. A potential solution is a population of uncorrelated neurons that, as a whole, can respond arbitrarily fast despite individual slow neurons. The response speed of a neuron or a population of neurons is often defined as how quickly neurons increase or decrease their firing rate given a change in the input, similar to a reaction time. Less emphasis is placed on the recovery time - the duration to transition and settle in a stationary state again in response to the change in the input. Here, we investigate the reaction time and the recovery time of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons given a change in, either the mean input drive, or input fluctuation level. In general, neurons react faster and fire quicker the larger the change in the input. Moreover, the closer the membrane potential is to the threshold, the faster the reaction. We observe that neurons react faster to increased input fluctuations than to stronger mean drive. Complementarily, the recovery time is systematically longer the larger the input change. Also, the closer the neurons' potentials are to the threshold, the longer it takes the neuron to recover. Most interestingly, the baseline firing of the neuron strongly determines whether recovery is faster when the change happens in the mean drive or the fluctuation level. This observation suggests that communication via the mean drive and the fluctuation level could target different aspects of the overall response - quick reaction time and the recovery speed - based on the initial baseline activity.

papers.title: Task-evoked flexibility of intrinsic neural timescales is hierarchically organized, behaviorally relevant, and refined across two developmental stages
papers.abstract: Cortical regions integrate temporal information over different timescales at rest, ranging from fast in sensorimotor regions to slow in the association cortex. Here, we study how far regions adapt these timescales to meet task demands, as well as how this emph{timescale flexibility} is organized across the cortical hierarchy, and how it develops in humans. We quantified rest-to-task changes in intrinsic neural timescales, referred to as emph{timescale deflections}, using fMRI data from four independent datasets totaling 1,712 participants aged 8--64 years. We found that timescales reduced under cognitive load in all four datasets, most strongly in association cortex, which partially flattened the resting-state timescale hierarchy. Individual differences in timescale deflections were organized along the sensorimotor-association (S-A) axis and tracked cognitive performance, both in adults and in youth. Next, in youth, deflections followed a two-stage developmental course: a generalized reduction throughout childhood, followed by a selective expansion in association cortex from mid-adolescence. Furthermore, the timing of these stages aligned with cortical gradients of inhibitory gene expression and intracortical myelin content, both features implicated in the opening and closing of critical periods of neural plasticity. Overall, our results demonstrate that task-evoked timescale flexibility is hierarchically organized, behaviorally and neurobiologically relevant, and refined across adolescence.

papers.title: Neuro-Metabolic and Vascular Dysregulation are Functional Biomarkers of Acquired Brain Injury
authors: J. A. K. H. Chong Chie
papers.abstract: Emerging clinical and neuropathological evidence suggests a direct link between traumatic brain injury (TBI) and neurodegenerative diseases (ND), but the mechanisms by which TBI contributes to ND onset and progression remain unclear. To bridge this gap, the NINDS TBI-ADRD consortium developed a diagnostic framework to guide the design and evaluation of TBI-ADRD experiments using translational neuroimaging (DCE-MRI, 18F-FDG-PET) and advanced image-processing pipelines. Neuro-metabolic and vascular dysregulation (MVD) and metabolic functional connectomics (MFC) were evaluated in 8-month C57BL/6J mice at 30- and 60-days post-injury (DPI). Both MVD and MFC revealed significant changes at 30- and 60-DPI that were sex- and injury side-dependent. Female mice showed greater regional MVD alterations, while MFC identified sex-dependent changes at 30-DPI that diminished by 60-DPI. These findings suggest that a single mid-life closed-head injury induces sexually dimorphic MVD and brain network remodeling, supporting the potential of MVD as a sensitive biomarker for improved clinical monitoring post-TBI.

papers.title: Sex-Dependent Effects of Creatine Hydrochloride on Neuroinflammation, Neuronal Survival, and Inhibitory Synaptic Remodeling Following Traumatic Brain Injury in Mice.
papers.abstract: Despite traumatic brain injury (TBI) being a leading cause of death and disability in the United States, there is currently no FDA-approved medication that can prevent, heal, or reverse brain damage caused by TBI. TBI is caused by primary and secondary brain damage resulting in loss of neurons, astrocytic gliosis, and microglial activation which culminate in complex neurological disorders. The goal of the current study was to investigate the neuroprotective potential for Creatine Hydrochloride (C-HCl) supplementation following TBI in wild-type mice. Four C-HCl supplementation paradigms were examined including both 7 day pre-injury and 14-day post-injury treatments consisting of the following: 1) water/water, 2) water/C-HCl (100 mg/kg), 3) C-HCl (100 mg/kg)/C-HCl (100 mg/kg), 4) C-HCl (100 mg/kg)/C-HCl (450 mg/kg). Following controlled cortical impact (CCI) injury at a parietal location, measures of tissue and cellular (neuronal and glial) damage were assessed at 14 days post-injury (dpi). At 14 dpi, there were no significant effects on gross anatomical cavitation, tissue loss, third ventricle expansion, or systemic fluid biomarkers with any treatment group, though female mice exhibited larger baseline lesion boundaries overall compared to male mice. However, microstructural evaluation revealed a profound and sex-dependent effect of C-HCl supplementation in the hippocampus with female mice showing reduced neuroinflammation and male mice displaying reduced neurodegeneration (Fluoro-Jade C staining of neurons) across the CA1 and dentate gyrus (DG) compared to placebo control. Furthermore, mice receiving C-HCl pre-injury followed by high-dose C-HCl post-injury demonstrated distinct remodeling of inhibitory circuits to restore network balance with males significantly modifying presynaptic machinery via vesicular GABA transport (VGAT puncta) in the DG, whereas females reinforced postsynaptic architectural framing through scaffolding elements (gephyrin puncta) in both the CA1 and DG. These results suggest C-HCl supplementation holds promise as a neuroprotective therapeutic strategy for TBI. Crucially, the molecular mechanisms utilized to achieve this brain cell homeostasis are radically distinct between the sexes, females benefit primarily via upstream glial stabilization, while males derive protection via direct downstream neuronal survival. These outcomes highlight a critical requirement for sex-stratified profiling in translational pipelines for neurometabolic interventions for TBI. Ultimately, these data indicate that C-HCl successfully counteracts chronic secondary injury cascades, mitigating neurodegeneration, dampening neuroinflammation, and remodeling inhibitory circuitry to prevent post-traumatic network hyperexcitability.

papers.title: Toward naturalistic reaching: Intermediate reaches under uncertainty generalize to walking, but are not obligatory
papers.abstract: Highly-constrained laboratory-based experiments have provided important insights into movement planning. When people reach toward one of several stimuli before knowing which to target, their hand trajectories are situated intermediate to direct reaches to each stimulus. Real-world reaching, however, involves a greater decision landscape than typical laboratory tasks. We extended the go-before-you-know paradigm to a walk-to-reach task resembling unconstrained natural behavior. Participants walked three steps toward a touchscreen before reaching for one of two stimuli, marked as the target either at walk onset or after reach onset. Under uncertainty, intermediate reaches occurred, but only for some stimulus layouts and participants. Individual reaches varied considerably; many directly targeted one stimulus and corrected late. Body position at reach onset was anchored to the screen more than the stimuli and was partly intermediate. Thus, intermediate movements generalize beyond the laboratory, but as one flexible strategy among several, not as obligatory motor plan averaging.

papers.title: A brain immune phenotype independent of Alzheimer's Disease associates with amyloid susceptibility and systemic inflammation
papers.abstract: Transcriptomic and proteomic studies have consistently demonstrated substantial molecular heterogeneity across patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative disorders, leading to the proposal of multiple disease subtypes. However, almost all previous studies have focused on heterogeneity within diseased cohorts, whereas comparatively little attention has been paid to the molecular diversity of neurologically healthy individuals. In the present study, we demonstrate that one of the most prominent transcriptomic programs characterized by a strong immune component previously interpreted as an AD-specific immune subtype is in fact a brain phenotype that exists independently of AD yet interacts with AD susceptibility and is selectively associated with amyloid pathology. The transcriptional effect of the immune phenotype exceeds that of AD pathology-induced changes and is accompanied by alterations of brain cellular compositions and a distinct systemic inflammation. Our findings suggest that part of the molecular heterogeneity observed in neurological diseases might arise from pre-existing brain phenotypes rather than representing disease-specific subtypes. These insights support a precision medicine approach for Alzheimer's disease, whereby individuals with an immune phenotype of the brain could be prospectively identified and monitored, enabling the application of targeted preventive strategies before substantial neuropathology and cognitive decline emerge.

papers.title: Spatial proximity to AD pathology defines cell-type and genotype-specific characteristics in human AD hippocampus
papers.abstract: How amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) plaques and tau phosphorylation spatially relate to cell response and genetic variation in Alzheimer's disease (AD) brain is currently unclear. We established a pipeline to concurrently annotate A{beta} and AT8 ptau pathology and cell-specific MERFISH expression profiles in human control and AD hippocampus. We characterized expression signatures in glia and neurons proximal or distal to A{beta} plaques, AT8 ptau-enriched neurons, or A{beta} and AT8 ptau in combination, and used spatially-defined transcriptional signatures to infer pathology-associated states in large snRNA-seq datasets lacking spatial context. We characterized variants from 120 gene loci associated with AD risk that affect cell-specific gene expression within local pathological contexts. Astrocyte APOE4/E4 expression was specifically suppressed in proximity to A{beta} plaques, whereas other APOE genotypes were unaffected by A{beta} proximity. Together, this analysis pipeline couples expression profiles in proximity to A{beta} and tau pathology, and implicates AD cis-gene variants with spatial sensitivity to AD pathology.

papers.title: Polyglutamine-expanded TBP rewires neuronal and muscle proteomes beyond transcription in a Drosophila model of SCA17
papers.abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 17 (SCA17) is an age-related neurodegenerative disorder caused by polyglutamine expansion in the TATA-binding protein (TBP). TBP is a core transcription factor, but pathogenic polyglutamine expansion likely rewires cellular programs beyond transcription. Here, we utilized Drosophila strains that express wild-type (WT) or pathogenic (SCA17) TBP in neurons or skeletal muscle, which we analyzed vs. controls via TMT mass spectrometry, profiling of eight post-translational modifications, and RNA-seq. Shared TBP-WT and TBP-SCA17 responses predominated, impacting ribosomes and mitochondria while repressing innate immunity. Disease-specific effects were narrower and tissue-dependent: SCA17 activated xenobiotic, retinoid, and glutathione-redox pathways in the CNS, but attenuated anabolism in muscle compared to TBP-WT. Many proteomic changes occurred independently of mRNA changes, implicating post-transcriptional mechanisms. Knockdown of select SCA17-regulated proteins reduced cytotoxicity, validating omics-identified modifiers of SCA17 pathology. These findings distinguish shared TBP dosage effects from disease-linked, tissue-specific polyglutamine responses and identify evolutionarily conserved targets for SCA17.

papers.title: Perceptual repulsion and decisional attraction in male body serial dependence: a dimensional dissociation in channel architecture
papers.abstract: Our judgments of the world are shaped by what we have just seen. This serial dependence is often treated as one bias, but it can constitute opposing influences: an attractive pull toward recent input and a repulsive push away from it. These have been linked to different stages, decisional and perceptual, but separated only for simple visual features. We asked whether the same separation holds for a socially significant category, the human body. Observers categorised images of male bodies as low or high on body fat and muscularity (binary choice, N = 74); a trial-level analysis estimated the perceptual and decisional contribution to each judgment. For body fat, the perceptual contribution was repulsive and clearly tuned, following a derivative-of-Gaussian profile peaking at a moderate difference between successive bodies ({sigma} {approx} 5.6 standardised units), while the decisional contribution was attractive; the dissociation held in most observers. Muscularity showed the same attractive decisional bias, but its perceptual tuning emerged only at longer viewing times, where its width approached that for body fat, indicating a difference in resolvability rather than an absence of tuning. To our knowledge, this is the first estimate of the tuning of the perceptual repulsion channels from binary categorisation of continuously varying stimuli, the first separation of perceptual and decisional components in body perception, and the first evidence of serial dependence for male bodies. Perception emphasises how a body differs from the previous one while the decision favours continuity, a division of labour spanning low-level features to high-level body judgments.

papers.title: Hippocampus mediates conceptual generalization of pain modulation
papers.abstract: Pain is strongly influenced by expectations and learning from previous experience, such as in classical conditioning. Conditioned responses and expectations can generalize to perceptually and conceptually related cues, but how generalization influences pain experience and the neurobiological processing of pain remains unclear. We used fMRI and multilevel mediation analyses to address this question. Thirty-six human participants first learned to associate two visual cues from distinct conceptual categories (e.g., animals vs. vehicles) with high or low levels of heat pain. In a subsequent phase, they were presented with novel cues (images, drawings, or words) not previously paired with pain, but which shared the conceptual category of the initial pain-predictive cues. Participants who developed explicit expectations during learning reported greater pain in response to stimuli conceptually related to high- vs. low-pain cues (generalization stimuli), demonstrating generalization of cue influences on pain. This effect was mediated by increased pain-related activity to generalization stimuli in the hippocampus, which correlated with individual differences in cue-evoked expectations. A broader network, including areas of the default mode network and striatum, also contributed to conceptual generalization of pain modulation, while threat-related regions such as the amygdala responded to generalization stimuli but did not mediate effects on pain ratings. These findings extend our understanding of expectancy-driven pain modulation by showing how conceptual processes can influence pain and its neurobiological substrates, offering new insight into placebo effects and maladaptive learning in chronic pain.

papers.title: Differential Survival of Retinal Ganglion Cell Types Following Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion
papers.abstract: Background. Branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) is a common cause of retinal ischemia, rapidly inducing neuronal death and often producing irreversible vison loss. Interventions such as thrombolysis restore perfusion but cannot recover neurons already lost, and most patients retain permanent visual deficits. Identifying which neuronal populations die, and how rapidly, may therefore reveal timing windows and targets for neuroprotective treatment. Aims. To determine the timing of pathology, we evaluated vascular changes and neuronal degeneration in a photocoagulation-induced mouse model of BRVO. To determine differences in retinal ganglion cells (RGC) type susceptibility, we tracked the survival of RGC subpopulations using immunofluorescence markers. Methods. BRVO was induced by retro-orbital injection of Rose Bengal and FITC dextran followed by targeted photocoagulation of a branch vein. Obstruction was confirmed by fluorescein angiography and vascular damage was viewed by optical coherence tomography angiography. Cell survival was quantified by immunostaining at 3, 7, and 14 days using RNA Binding Protein with Multiple Splicing (RBPMS, pan RGC). RGC subtype markers for intrinsically photosensitive RGCs (TBR2), RGCs (SPP1), ON OFF direction-selective RGCs (CART), and F RGCs (FOXP2) were used to examine differences in survival across RGC types. Results. Occlusion selectively disrupted the superficial and intermediate capillary plexus, sparing the deep plexuses. All examined neuronal populations were significantly depleted, but with markedly different magnitude and timing. RGCs and F RGCs were the most vulnerable subtypes, both approaching complete loss by one week, whereas intrinsically photosensitive RGCs were the most resistant. Conclusion. RGCs, typically resilient in glaucoma, trauma, and excitotoxicity, were markedly vulnerable in BRVO, indicating that RGC subtype susceptibility is insult-specific.

papers.title: The marginal brain
papers.abstract: Goal-directed cognition raises brain energy use only a few percent above resting use, a figure often read as evidence that cognition is metabolically cheap. Models of endogenous precision derive the precision of neural representations from a cost on encoding activity whose unit price is a free parameter. Embedding endogenous precision in a regulated, shared energy budget makes this cost the shadow price of energy at the margin of the budget. Neither the task share of the budget nor the net whole-brain increment identifies this price; when tasks face a common price ratio and coding technology is stable, imprecision changes by the exact fourth root of that ratio, so that the cost of information rescales while its shape is preserved; and the co-movement of imprecision and stimulus-linked task energy separates price changes from changes in coding technology. In 12,960 published estimation trials, response variance at matched numerosities rises with prior width in line with the ratios that the calibrated model predicts out of sample, and simulations indicate that a doubled price is detectable with existing paradigms when state-dependent lapses are modeled.

papers.title: The human hippocampus retroactively binds experiences across time
papers.abstract: Creating memories requires linking events across seconds and minutes, but canonical mechanisms of associative plasticity operate over much shorter timescales. This poses a fundamental problem: how can the brain bind information that arrives at different times? Computational model and animal studies implicate the hippocampus in associating events across time, but when the hippocampus becomes engaged and how it interacts with representations of preceding events are unknown. Here we show, using intracranial recordings in humans forming image-word associations across a ~2-s temporal gap, that hippocampal high-frequency activity predicts later memory when the second event arrives, but not during the initial image or intervening delay. At this moment, neurons tuned to the preceding image reinstate stimulus-specific firing despite its sensory absence. Across trials, hippocampal high-frequency activity was selectively coupled to this reinstatement during successful encoding and increased before spiking of image-tuned neurons. These findings reveal a retroactive mode of hippocampal binding, whereby representations of preceding events are recruited when new information arrives. This mechanism provides a neural solution for binding experiences across the temporal discontinuities that characterize everyday life.

papers.title: Social brain fingerprinting: unique functional connectomes underpin interpersonal behaviours in non-autistic and autistic adults
papers.abstract: Human social interaction requires continuous adaptation while preserving stable individual patterns of brain organisation. This study examined whether functional connectome fingerprinting captures person-specific organisation during reciprocal interaction and whether its spatial architecture relates to social role and autistic traits. fMRI data from 70 adults forming 35 dyads were analysed during an iterated Ultimatum Game: 19 non-autistic Proposer-non-autistic Responder dyads and 16 non-autistic Proposer-autistic Responder dyads. Functional connectivity across 400 cortical parcels was used to assess whole-brain identifiability and edge-wise reliability. Connectomes remained identifiable across datasets, roles, and task conditions, with no reduction in global identifiability in mixed dyads. Edge-wise analyses revealed role-related and dataset-dependent differences across distributed large-scale networks. Role-sensitive connectivity features were associated with Autism-Spectrum Quotient scores, supported out-of-sample prediction, and topology-derived features classified AQ-threshold status above chance. Stable connectomic signatures therefore persist during reciprocal interaction while their network organisation varies with social role and autistic traits.

papers.title: LLM-assisted analytical review catches statistical errors that human researchers miss: documented evidence from two computational biology case studies
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assist with code generation and data analysis in computational biology, but their capacity to serve as analytical reviewers -- detecting statistical and methodological errors in completed analyses -- is less documented. We present two case studies in which LLM-assisted review identified consequential errors in computational biology analyses that the human researchers had not detected. In single-cell transcriptomics, review of a differential expression analysis of 22,048 cells from human striatum identified a sex composition confound (Chi-squared = 192.7, p = 8.1 x 10-44) that had produced spurious Y-chromosome gene hits; correction revealed KIF3A as the sole genuine finding (adjusted p = 1.37 x 10-14). In HRV-based stress classification, review identified subject leakage in a train-test split that allowed the same individuals in training and test sets; correction via leave-one-subject-out cross-validation produced a more reliable and higher AUC estimate (0.946 vs. 0.848). Both errors would have survived conventional peer review in the absence of systematic checking. Both corrected analyses have been submitted for peer review. These cases suggest that LLM-assisted analytical review -- using LLMs to interrogate completed analyses for confounds, leakage, and statistical artifacts -- is a practical quality assurance step that complements rather than replaces human scientific judgment.
